details:
**Tartuffe**
Molière's most famous play (1664), about a falsely pious religious hypocrite and "impostor" who worms his way into the household of the wealthy, gullible Orgon. It is the near-universal giveaway for Molière, and it was banned for years after protests from religious authorities.

**Orgon hides under a table while Elmire is seduced**
The most famous scene of Tartuffe. Orgon's wife Elmire persuades her skeptical husband to hide under a cloth-covered table so he can witness Tartuffe making advances on her, finally proving the man's hypocrisy.

**Louis XIV's intervention and Tartuffe's arrest**
Tartuffe ends with a deus ex machina: after Tartuffe has gained the deed to Orgon's house and a strongbox of incriminating letters belonging to Orgon's friend, an officer sent by King Louis XIV, Molière's patron, arrests Tartuffe and restores the family's property.

**Damis, Mariane, Valère, and Madame Pernelle**
Members of Orgon's family in Tartuffe. Damis, Orgon's son, reports Tartuffe's attempted seduction but is disbelieved, banished, and disinherited in Tartuffe's favor. Orgon tries to marry his daughter Mariane to Tartuffe, though she loves Valère, whom she marries at the end. Orgon's mother Madame Pernelle is as fooled by Tartuffe as he is, while Orgon's brother-in-law Cléante serves as the voice of reason.

**Monsieur Loyal and Panulphe**
Monsieur Loyal is the bailiff who arrives to evict Orgon's family, and he is mocked for his ironic name. Panulphe was the title character's name in the revised 1667 version of Tartuffe (titled The Impostor), which was also banned, with threats of excommunication for anyone who saw or read it.

**The Misanthrope**
Molière's 1666 comedy about Alceste, a brutally honest man who despises the flattery and hypocrisy of society. His reasonable friend Philinte argues for tact, and the play is often called Molière's masterpiece.

**Oronte's sonnet**
In The Misanthrope, the fop Oronte asks Alceste's opinion of a sonnet he has written. Alceste mocks it as terrible, and Oronte sues him over the insult, bringing Alceste before a tribunal.

**Célimène**
The witty, flirtatious young widow loved by Alceste in The Misanthrope. She is courted by several suitors, including Oronte, Acaste, and Clitandre, and is exposed when her letters mocking each of them are read aloud. When she refuses to follow Alceste into isolation, he leaves society to live as a hermit.

**The Imaginary Invalid and Molière's death**
Molière's final play (1673) is about the hypochondriac Argan. Molière collapsed while playing Argan during its fourth performance and died a few hours later, an often-cited irony.

**Argan, Toinette, and Thomas Diafoirus**
In The Imaginary Invalid, Argan wants his daughter Angélique to marry the foolish doctor-to-be Thomas Diafoirus so he can get free medical care, though she loves Cléante. The maid Toinette disguises herself as a doctor (advising Argan to cut off an arm and poke out an eye) and has Argan pretend to be dead, revealing that his second wife Béline only wants his money while Angélique truly loves him. The play ends with Argan himself becoming a doctor in a ceremony in mock Latin.

**The School for Wives**
Molière's 1662 comedy in which the middle-aged Arnolphe raises his ward Agnès in ignorance (she asks if babies come from the ear) so that she will be an obedient wife. His plans fail when she falls for the young Horace and marries him. Molière defended the play in The Critique of The School for Wives, and William Wycherley drew on it for The Country Wife.

**The Bourgeois Gentleman**
Molière's 1670 comedy-ballet about Monsieur Jourdain, the social-climbing son of a cloth merchant who hires tutors in music, dancing, fencing, and philosophy. He is famously delighted to learn he has been speaking prose all his life, and he is tricked into a fake Turkish ceremony while his daughter Lucile marries Cléonte, who is disguised as the son of the Sultan of Turkey.

**The Miser**
Molière's 1668 comedy about the stingy Harpagon. His son Cléante competes with him for Mariane, and Cléante's valet La Flèche steals a box of money Harpagon has buried in his garden. The play ends when Anselme reveals that he is Don Thomas d'Alburcy and the long-lost father of Mariane and Valère, who survived a shipwreck.

**The Doctor in Spite of Himself and Sganarelle**
In this 1666 farce, Martine gets revenge on her drunken woodcutter husband Sganarelle by telling a rich man's servants that he is a brilliant doctor who will only admit it if beaten. Sganarelle is a recurring Molière character who also appears as Don Juan's servant in Molière's Dom Juan.

**The Affected Young Ladies and Amphitryon**
The Affected Young Ladies (Les Précieuses ridicules) satirizes the pretentious cousins Magdelon and Cathos, daughter and niece of Gorgibus, who reject their suitors, including La Grange. Molière's adaptation of Plautus's Amphitryon gave French the word "sosie" (look-alike), from the servant Sosie.
